A baptism or christening record for Caroline Voss (born 1839, window widened slightly for birth-year uncertainty) would name both parents directly and is the most compact form of parentage evidence. **Mode:** create — first plan for q_001 ("Who were the parents of Patrick Flynn (b. ~1845, PA, d. 1908)?")

**Tree survey findings that bear on the question:**
- Patrick Flynn (I1): Birth ~1845 recorded as **Ireland** (F1), not Pennsylvania — family emigrated from Ireland before the 1850 census; Death 1908-03-12, Schuylkill County, PA (F2, sourced from death cert S3, cert. no. 4521)
- Thomas Flynn (I2): Birth ~1818, Ireland (F3, no source attached); listed as head of household in 1850 and 1860 censuses; currently the only parent in the tree for Patrick
- Relationship R1 (Thomas → Patrick): sourced by S1 (1850 census), S2 (1860 census), and S3 (death cert) — but the underlying assertions a_004 and a_005 are both inferred from co-residence and shared surname, not stated relationships; zero assertions from S3 have been extracted for q_001
- S4 (Schuylkill County Probate Records): in the tree's source list but not referenced by any fact or relationship — identified but not searched

---

**Plan pl_002, 8 items in execution order:**

| # | Item | Record Type | Place | Date Range | Repository |
|---|------|-------------|-------|------------|------------|
| 1 | pli_004 | vital_record (death cert) | Schuylkill County, PA | 1908 | FamilySearch |
| 2 | pli_005 | probate | Schuylkill County, PA | 1850–1905 | FamilySearch |
| 3 | pli_006 | church (indexed) | Schuylkill County, PA | 1840–1910 | FamilySearch |
| 4 | pli_007 | census (1870–1880) | Schuylkill County, PA | 1870–1880 | FamilySearch |
| 5 | pli_008 | vital_record (marriage) | Schuylkill County, PA | 1865–1907 | FamilySearch |
| 6 | pli_009 | church (browse-only) | Schuylkill County, PA | 1842–1895 | FamilySearch (fallback from pli_006) |
| 7 | pli_010 | court (naturalization) | Schuylkill County, PA | 1845–1880 | FamilySearch |
| 8 | pli_011 | immigration | US Atlantic ports | 1840–1850 | Ancestry |

**Rationale by item:**
- **pli_004** — The 1908 PA death certificate (already in the tree as S3) has never been extracted for q_001; Pennsylvania death certs from 1906+ carry informant-stated father's name and mother's maiden name — the most direct route to naming both parents.
- **pli_005** — S4 (Schuylkill County Probate Records) is in the source list but attached to no fact; a will or administration for Thomas Flynn would name heirs and possibly his wife.
- **pli_006** — The indexed PA church collection (982,415 persons) covers 19th-century vital records; search for Thomas Flynn's marriage and any Flynn baptisms.
- **pli_007** — The 1880 census explicitly states the relationship of each person to the head, upgrading the parentage from inferred to directly reported; FAN households in the same district may be Patrick's siblings.
- **pli_008** — Marriage records for Patrick commonly named the groom's father as surety or in the license body.
- **pli_009** — Browse-only fallback church volume if pli_006 returns nothing.
- **pli_010** — Thomas's naturalization declaration likely recorded his Irish county/townland and possibly his wife's name.
- **pli_011** — Pre-1850 passenger lists sometimes recorded family groups; finding Thomas with a wife and child named Patrick would establish the mother's name and Irish origin.

**Total scope:** 8 items; 7 FamilySearch searches + 1 Ancestry external search.

**Note on Irish records:** Patrick's baptism, if it exists, is in Ireland. No specific parish is yet known; pli_010 and pli_011 are most likely to supply the Irish locality needed for a follow-on Irish records plan.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

Thomas Flynn (born ~1818 Ireland) appears in the 1850 Schuylkill County census, so he immigrated to the United States before 1850 and would typically have filed a declaration of intent or completed naturalization within the following decade. Naturalization papers in this period frequently named the petitioner's wife and minor children, providing independent evidence of family membership. Date window is bound by the siblings' plausible lifespans, not Patrick's.

Fallback for the probate search (pli_006): if Thomas Flynn died intestate or if the probate image browse yields no record, land deeds may still name his heirs in a conveyance or provide boundary recitals naming adjoining landowners (neighbors who are FAN sources). Volume 007936752 (Schuylkill County deed records 1815-1900) is 22% record-searchable; a name search for Thomas Flynn covers deeds he executed as grantor or grantee. quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright by laborers.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) -- browse image-by-image.
Curated external links reach county tax and exoneration lists for 1768-1801 only, before this period.

Finding Michael — and variants Sheehan and Shehan — in 1870 establishes his county of residence a full decade before the move, his household composition (whether brother Patrick was then with him), and his occupation before the anthracite coal region drew him to Schuylkill County.

FAN item targeting Patrick Sheahan (I2), Michael's brother. Source S1 already in the project documents Patrick purchasing land in Schuylkill County in 1875 (Deed Book 42, p. 118) — seven years before Michael's documented 1882 arrival. The 1880 census is name-searchable and should show Patrick resident and employed in Schuylkill County while Michael was still elsewhere. An established sibling working in the anthracite mines is a classic chain-migration pull factor; confirming Patrick's occupation and township in 1880 speaks directly to why Michael followed him to the county. Also search variants Sheehan and Shehan.

Sheahan is an Irish surname associated with County Cork and Kerry; Michael is likely Roman Catholic. The localities entry confirms Schuylkill County Catholic parishes were under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875). collections_search returned Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records, which is name-searchable (personCount 982,415), covering 1708-1985. A sacramental or membership-transfer entry placing Michael in a county parish would approximate his arrival date; an entry predating 1882 would indicate the move was earlier than the tree records. Some church registers for the coal region are also available as a browse-only image group (volume 007936751, 1842-1895, personCount 0 per volume_search) — if the name-searchable collection returns nothing, browse that volume image-by-image. The record may also name Michael's sending parish, which is direct evidence of his geographic origin.

If Michael Sheahan was born in Ireland and immigrated before 1882, he would have filed a declaration of intent or petition for naturalization in the county where he settled. volume_search returned a Schuylkill County Naturalization Records image group (007936750, 1849-1915) that is browse-only (personCount 0) — the localities entry confirms some naturalization films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only and must be examined image-by-image. Naturalization records routinely state occupation, birthplace, port and year of arrival, and country of origin — exactly the evidence needed to confirm whether employment in the anthracite mines drove the immigration and where Michael was before arriving in Schuylkill County.

The 1900 US census (collections_search returned United States Census, 1900, name-searchable, personCount above 0) asks for immigration year, number of years in the United States, and nativity — details absent from earlier census years. Finding Michael in Schuylkill County in 1900 with occupation Miner, plus his stated immigration year, would directly confirm mining work as the sustained occupation after the move and establish whether he arrived in the US directly to Schuylkill County or first settled elsewhere in Pennsylvania. Also search variants Sheehan and Shehan.

entry.repository: Pennsylvania State Archives / Historical Society of Schuylkill County
entry.rationale: Anthracite colliery operators were required to file reports with Pennsylvania's Bureau of Mines from 1870; mine employment payroll records and colliery books were kept by individual operators. The Miners' Journal (Pottsville, PA) is the regional newspaper of record for the anthracite coal region and reported mine employment, accidents, strikes, and community news. Neither source is available through FamilySearch or Ancestry. Holdings are at the Pennsylvania State Archives (record group for Bureau of Mines reports) and the Historical Society of Schuylkill County (Pottsville). A colliery payroll entry or a mine-employment record naming Michael Sheahan would be the strongest possible direct confirmation of the family tradition that he came for anthracite coal-mining work.

S1 already in the project shows Patrick Sheahan purchased land in Schuylkill County in 1875. If Michael also acquired property after arriving, a deed would confirm his settlement in the county and could name neighboring landowners (FAN), further corroborating the permanence of the move.   This plan addresses whether Michael Sheahan moved to Schuylkill County around 1882 for coal-mining work. Because every fact currently recorded for him — his 1870 Pennsylvania residence, his 1882 Schuylkill County residence, and his occupation as a miner — is in the family tree without any source document behind it, the plan starts by verifying those bare facts with real records. It searches the 1880 federal census first (just two years before the stated move, and the quickest way to see where he actually was and what work he was doing), then steps back to the 1870 census to trace the earlier trajectory, and forward to the 1900 census, which uniquely recorded how long immigrants had been in the country — a direct test of the family tradition. Church records for the county's Catholic parishes follow, since colliery-town parishes formed the heart of immigrant mining communities and a sacramental entry would pin him to a specific mining village. Naturalization papers come next: if Michael was Irish-born, his declaration of intention or petition would record exactly when he arrived in the United States and where he was living in Schuylkill County. A search of all Sheahan households in the county's census records runs alongside those items to check whether relatives or townspeople preceded him — chain migration from Ireland drove most Irish labor movement into the Pennsylvania anthracite fields, and an earlier Sheahan presence would explain why he chose this county. Pennsylvania death certificates close the plan as a backup source that names occupation and birthplace when the census and naturalization records do not resolve the question.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

**Question:** Who were the parents of Patrick Flynn (b. ~1845, PA, d. 1908)?

---

| # | Record type | Place / date | Repository | Method |
|---|-------------|--------------|------------|--------|

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.

The national collection 'United States Census, 1860' (1473181) is name-searchable; a search filtered to Georgia for a Wood head of household with a young female child (~age 1, born in Georgia) is the test. This is a fallback if the Blount County, Alabama census search yields nothing usable — either because the uncited tree source is wrong about the state, or because the family was still in Georgia at census time.

Dedicated search for the parents' marriage, keyed on the surname 'Wood' (from a_003, Martha's 1869 Smith County Texas marriage as 'M J Wood'). The parents' marriage confirms them as a couple and — if this was the mother's first marriage — supplies her maiden name, the key identifier absent from all later records of Martha. Even if not the mother's first union, the record dates the couple's connection and corroborates any father named only by indirect or derivative evidence. Reviewing the image is a free FAN step on a record already held. The Smith County marriage volumes 007255720 and 007255721 (loc_002) are 100% name-indexed and full-text searchable. Martha's parents would appear in the 1850 census as a young couple — possibly with early children, but before Martha's ~1859 birth. A search for 'Wood' households in Georgia in 1850 whose head's age is consistent with having a child born in 1859 establishes the parents' names and birthplaces before Martha's birth, and any siblings found there confirm the family unit. Alabama had no civil birth or death registration before 1908 (loc_001 quirk). Baptist and Methodist church records are the primary substitute in Blount County. items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

Completing the 1900 search closes the final unexamined census decade for Patrick's adult life. Thomas Flynn (b. ~1818 Ireland) likely died sometime after the 1860 census. The upper bound of the search window is set by Thomas's plausible lifespan: born ~1818, death plausible through approximately 1898. A will or estate administration naming Patrick as a son would be direct parentage evidence. Per loc_001, probate at the Schuylkill County Register of Wills is available from 1811; the county was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton Counties. Thomas Flynn's marriage to Patrick's mother: (a) establishes the couple as a unit; (b) supplies the mother's maiden name, which census and death records do not record; (c) by its date relative to Patrick's birth (~1845), corroborates Thomas as Patrick's father. items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been located. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright by laborers.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) -- browse image-by-image.
Curated external links reach county tax and exoneration lists for 1768-1801 only, before this period.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
